lessons.title: Who is speaking?
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Who is speaking?: Yo means I, tú means informal you, and usted means formal you.
lessons.focus: Use être for “am / is / are”: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Peers often use tu right away; use vous with a teacher, staff member, or an adult stranger, and keep one register in a conversation. A mixed group uses ils, and masculine plural étudiants; an all-female group uses elles and étudiantes. In est the final t is usually silent, but it links before a vowel in il est ici; the t in êtes is pronounced.
lessons.scene: Before class at a language school, Nadia meets Hugo, a classmate. They use tu with each other, and Hugo points out where the teacher is.
dialogue: Hugo: Salut ! Tu es Nadia ?|Hi! Are you Nadia?
Nadia: Oui, je suis Nadia. Et toi, tu es Hugo ?|Yes, I am Nadia. And you, are you Hugo?
Hugo: Oui, je suis Hugo. Nous sommes étudiants ici.|Yes, I am Hugo. We are students here.
Nadia: Ah, d’accord ! Et le professeur, il est ici ?|Oh, okay! And the teacher, is he here?
Hugo: Oui, il est là. Il est très gentil.|Yes, he is there. He is very kind.
Nadia: Et Léa et Tom ?|And Léa and Tom?
Hugo: Ils sont étudiants aussi.|They are students too.
Nadia: Parfait. Merci, Hugo !|Perfect. Thanks, Hugo!
Hugo: De rien, Nadia. À demain !|You’re welcome, Nadia. See you tomorrow!
lessons.speaking: Role-play meeting a classmate before class, using tu throughout. Opening: say Salut ! and ask Tu es plus the classmate’s name. Task 1: say who you are with Je suis plus your name, then ask Et toi, tu es ... ?. Task 2: say that you are both students with Nous sommes étudiants ici. Task 3: point to a teacher or classmate and say Il est là or Elle est là, matching that person, then point to a mixed group and say Ils sont étudiants for a mixed group (or Elles sont étudiantes for a group of women). Closure: say Merci and close with À demain ! Your partner uses tu throughout, repeats any unclear word, and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.

lessons.title: Who am I? Identity and origin
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Ser: identity and origin: Use ser for identity, origin and characteristics.
lessons.focus: Use être for roles and traits: je suis étudiant or étudiante; il est gentil, elle est gentille. A role normally has no article after être: je suis étudiante. Learn the noun or adjective ending for the person described. Learn Je viens de as a fixed origin chunk for now: de France for a feminine country, d’Espagne before a vowel, du Canada for a masculine country, and des États-Unis for a plural country. Country articles matter; do not apply de to every country.
lessons.scene: At the sign-in table of a language café, Claire and Marc, who met in Lesson 1, share who they are and where they come from.
dialogue: Claire: Bonjour, Marc ! Vous êtes étudiant ici ?|Hello, Marc! Are you a student here?
Marc: Oui, je suis étudiant. Et vous, vous êtes étudiante ?|Yes, I am a student. And you, are you a student?
Claire: Oui, je suis étudiante. Je viens d’Espagne.|Yes, I am a student. I come from Spain.
Marc: Ah, je viens de France. Et la professeure ?|Oh, I come from France. And the teacher?
Claire: Elle est française. Elle est gentille.|She is French. She is kind.
Marc: Merci ! Au revoir, Claire.|Thank you! Goodbye, Claire.
Claire: Au revoir, Marc !|Goodbye, Marc!
lessons.speaking: Role-play meeting another adult learner at a language café using vous throughout. Open with Bonjour and ask Vous êtes étudiant(e) ici ? State your role with Je suis étudiant or étudiante. Say your origin using one taught chunk: de France, d’Espagne, du Canada, or des États-Unis. If your country is different, ask the partner in English for its French form rather than guessing. Ask about a teacher and describe that person with il/elle est gentil/gentille or français/française. Close with Merci and Au revoir. Your partner uses vous and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.

lessons.title: Where is it? Location and state
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Estar: location and condition: Use estar for a person's or object's location and for conditions.
lessons.focus: Use être for the locations and states in this lesson: Le livre est sur la table; La porte est ouverte. Some other everyday states use avoir (for example, j’ai faim); those come later. Sur means on, dans means in, and près de means near; before le, de + le becomes du (près du livre), and before les it becomes des (here meaning de + les, distinct from the indefinite article des). For a thing, il replaces a masculine noun and elle a feminine noun: le livre → il, la trousse → elle. Adjectives agree with the noun or person: le livre est ouvert, la porte est ouverte; Marc est fatigué, Claire est fatiguée.
lessons.scene: At a shared classroom table, Claire and Marc look for a book and a pen, then decide whether they are ready to leave.
dialogue: Claire: Marc, où est le livre ?|Marc, where is the book?
Marc: Il est sur la table.|It is on the table.
Claire: Et la trousse ?|And the pencil case?
Marc: Elle est sur la table.|It is on the table.
Claire: Et le stylo ? Il est dans la trousse ?|And the pen? Is it in the pencil case?
Marc: Non, il est près du livre.|No, it is near the book.
Claire: Ah, merci ! Et vous, vous êtes fatigué ?|Ah, thanks! And you, are you tired?
Marc: Oui, je suis fatigué. Et vous, vous êtes prête ?|Yes, I am tired. And you, are you ready?
Claire: Oui, je suis prête. La porte est ouverte !|Yes, I am ready. The door is open!
lessons.speaking: Role-play finding objects in a classroom with an adult learner you have just met; use vous throughout. Open with Où est le stylo ? Answer using sur la table, dans la trousse, or près du livre (de + le → du). Ask where the trousse is and answer with Elle est... because trousse is feminine. Say Je suis fatigué/fatiguée and ask Vous êtes prêt/prête ? matching the person; then describe La porte est ouverte. Close with Merci and Au revoir. Your partner repeats unclear words and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.
